Seif 1. "One who buries his dead during the festival: mourning does not take effect upon him during the festival," etc. A case came before me involving a person who became a mourner during Sukkot, may the Merciful One spare us, and I ruled that he may receive an aliyah on Simchat Torah.

The reason is that the universal custom is for everyone to receive an aliyah on Simchat Torah. If the mourner alone does not receive one, his mourning becomes publicly apparent. One might distinguish this from the case in which Rabbeinu Tam was ordinarily accustomed to receive an aliyah in that place, so that his failure to do so would be public, whereas here perhaps people could assume the mourner already received an aliyah elsewhere. Maharshal, responsum 71, writes similarly regarding a mourner who is the father of an infant receiving brit milah and nevertheless does not receive an aliyah.

However, there is another reason to permit it. Shulchan Aruch states that on Erev Rosh Hashanah a mourner may leave his house in order to recite Selichot. Although on other days a mourner may not leave, because everyone increases Selichot then it would cause him distress to remain at home. The same reasoning applies on Simchat Torah. Since all Israel customarily receives aliyot, it causes the mourner distress to sit aside and not receive one. This resembles the permission to leave his house for Selichot.

There is an additional consideration based on Taz, Hilchot Shabbos, siman 244, concerning marit ayin. Taz writes that where there are 2 possible grounds for assuming permission, one may rely upon appearances; where there is only 1, we may be concerned that observers know that ground does not apply and will therefore suspect a prohibition.

Regarding a mourner whose son is receiving brit milah, there are 2 grounds upon which observers may explain why he did not receive an aliyah: perhaps they do not know that today is his son's brit milah, in which case he had no special reason to receive an aliyah; and even if they know, perhaps he already received an aliyah in another synagogue. There are thus 2 possibilities and no necessary public manifestation of mourning.

On Simchat Torah, however, because everyone receives an aliyah, there is only 1 possible explanation for his not receiving one, namely that perhaps he already did so elsewhere. Many people may know that he did not, and will then recognize that he is refraining because of mourning. That becomes a public practice of mourning.

It is true that one could distinguish our case from Taz's case and argue that it still does not constitute true public mourning. Nevertheless, this entire matter is rabbinic, especially during a festival when the laws of mourning do not take effect, and there is also the consideration of the distress caused to the mourner. Therefore one should be lenient in such a case. This is clear and correct as practical halacha.
